newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina heading for moderate growth cycle.
newsitem.headline: Argentina heading for moderate growth cycle.

text.p: Argentina is poised to enter a new expansionary cycle in 1997, but the high growth rates of 1991 to 1994 will not be repeated, analysts say.
The economy is seen benefitting from positive international trends, with low U.S. interest rates and high liquidity levels, rising exports and growing bank credit.
"Even though the growth cycle is a reality, the figures for 1997 growth are likely to be four or five percent and not 10 percent," said Daniel Artana, an economist at the FIEL private consultancy.

Argentine growth averaged 8.9 percent annually from the launch of the Convertibility plan in 1991, pegging the value of the peso to the dollar at par, until the Mexican devaluation at the end of 1994.

But in 1995 the country was hit by a hard recession produced by fears around the strength of Convertibility and its vulnerability to external shocks, highlighted by low domestic savings rates which worsened the dependency on overseas financing.
In 1996 there has been a rebound which has sufficed to push industrial production back up to its levels at the end of 1994 but failed to bump it up to pre "Tequila" levels.

"The conditions are in place for expansion, but at a lower rate than before the crisis, since consumption, which makes up a large part of aggregate demand, will grow less than gross domestic product," said Nicolas Dujovne, an economist at Macroeconomica. However, analysts warn of possible fiscal shortfalls in 1997, caused by political softness ahead of next year's mid-term congressional elections and the tendency to raise public expenditures.

For example, private consultancy C&E Consultores reckons the most likely scenario is that there will be three percent growth in 1997, "keeping in mind the slowdown in growth in the second half caused by political conflicts."

Meanwhile, Jose Luis Espert, head of consultants Econometrica, warns: "The quality of this growth will not be very healthy because essentially we are heading towards a situation of pushing the fiscal deficit which will be financed by more debt."

"We made the same mistake in the previous growth cycle, which was to relax fiscal discipline and raise debt during periods in which there were privatizations. Now we cannot count on these sales and I think the deficit will continue to grow."
The deficit this year is expected to be $6.0 billion.

Public debt is expected to grow to $100 billion in 1996, amounting to five times the value of exports, compared with less than $75 billion in 1991. But within the possible scenarios, the analysts emphasize that their forecasts do not count on the possibility of a crisis in Brazil.
"Our worst case scenario contemplates a return of the recession...that can be produced by one of two factors: an external or an internal crisis," said C&E.
"The first could come from the impact of a crisis in Brazil, where the macroeconomic imbalances could cause a devaluation and provoke a run on our market and bank deposits."
C&E reckons an internal crisis, meanwhile, could come as a consequence of a return to political populism, caused for example by a massive defeat by the Peronist government in next year's elections.
